title: How to ask a question that actually gets answered
body:
Getting a good answer starts before you hit publish. The questions that get real, useful answers on this community share a few habits.

**Be specific about your situation.** "How do I fix my WiFi?" is nearly unanswerable — nobody knows your router, your provider, or what you have already tried. "My WiFi drops every evening around 7pm on a Jio router, restarting it fixes it for a few hours" gives an answerer something to actually work with.

**Show what you already tried.** If you searched first and found a suggestion that did not work, say so. It saves everyone from repeating the same dead end, and it signals you have put in effort.

**One question per post.** "Which laptop should I buy and also how do I invest my savings" is really two questions competing for the same answer. Split them, and each gets a focused response from someone who actually knows that topic.

**Add context, not just symptoms.** Budget, location, timeline, constraints — the details that make advice specific to you rather than generic. "Best phone under 15000" gets a worse answer than "Best phone under 15000 for someone who mainly uses the camera and WhatsApp."

None of this is complicated, and it takes maybe thirty extra seconds to write. That thirty seconds is usually the difference between three vague replies and one answer that actually solves your problem.
excerpt: A few small habits separate questions that get real answers from ones that get silence.
meta_description: How to write a question that gets a useful answer, not just a reply.

title: Why we show reputation points on every profile
body:
Every answer, upvote and accepted answer on this platform feeds into a single number on your profile: reputation. It is worth explaining what it actually represents, because it is easy to mistake it for a leaderboard when it is really a trust signal.

Reputation exists to answer one question for a stranger reading your answer: has this person been useful to other people before? A new account and a 5,000-point account might both post a correct answer, but the second one has a track record a reader can actually check.

**It is earned slowly on purpose.** A handful of points per accepted answer, a smaller amount per upvote — the system deliberately resists being gamed by one viral post. Consistency over time is what it is measuring, not a single lucky answer.

**It unlocks very little, deliberately.** Reputation is not a paywall or a rank system with special privileges — it stays a visible history of contribution, not a gate other users have to get past.

**It is public because trust needs to be checkable.** You can look at anyone's reputation history and see exactly which answers earned it, because a trust score nobody can verify is not actually trustworthy — it is just a number someone is asked to take on faith.

If you are new here, do not worry about your number. Answer the questions you actually know something about, and the number takes care of itself.
excerpt: Reputation is a public, checkable record of whether someone's answers have actually helped people before.
meta_description: What reputation points mean here, and why the system is built the way it is.

title: Reading the community guidelines, the short version
body:
The full guidelines page covers a lot of ground, but almost all of it comes down to three ideas. If you only remember these, you are in good shape.

**Answer the question that was actually asked.** Not the question you wish had been asked, not a chance to promote something unrelated. If someone asks how to do X, either help them do X or explain clearly why X is not a good idea — and then help with what they actually need.

**Disagree with the answer, not the person.** "That approach has a problem with Y, here's why" moves a conversation forward. Attacking the person who wrote it does not, and it makes the next person less likely to answer honestly at all.

**When you are not sure, say so.** "I have not done this myself, but I believe..." is a genuinely useful contribution. Confident-sounding guesses presented as fact are the fastest way to erode trust in every other answer on the page, including the correct ones.

Everything in the full guidelines exists to protect those three things, not to add rules for their own sake.
excerpt: Almost everything in the full guidelines comes down to three ideas: answer what was asked, disagree with the argument not the person, and say when you are unsure.
meta_description: The community guidelines, condensed to the three ideas that actually matter.
